pew_item: Do you favor or oppose raising the federal minimum wage to $15.00 an hour?
notes: Federal $15 minimum wage, not a local increase. Question wording and the 62% overall come from the topline PDF (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Minimum-Wage-topline-for-release.pdf). Partisan groups include leaners. The page gives Rep/lean Rep only as 72% oppose (45% strongly oppose), with no Rep favor figure, so rep_lean_rep is left out. Favor among Republicans by income: lower 46, middle 23, upper 18. By household income: lower 72, middle 58, upper 55. No gender, age, religion or geography breakdown on the page.

pew_item: Do you favor or oppose the following proposals to reduce the effects of global climate change? b. Taxing corporations based on the amount of carbon emissions they produce
notes: A national tax on corporations by emissions, not a regional carbon fee; the item asks favor/oppose, not whether it helps growth. Partisan groups include leaners (chart labels Rep/lean Rep, Dem/lean Dem). Party trend 2020/21/22/23: Rep 55/50/46/50, Dem 89/87/86/89. Overall trend: 73 (2020), 70 (2021), 68 (2022), 70 (2023). A newer reading (Oct 21-27, 2024; https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2024/12/09/how-americans-view-climate-change-and-policies-to-address-the-issue/) has 68% overall and Rep 47%, but no exact Dem figure, so 2023 is used. The same 2024 report has an economy item closer to the claim: climate policies 'usually help the economy' 34% overall, Rep/lean Rep 16, Dem/lean Dem 52 ('hurt': 34 / 56 / 13). The Rep and Dem 'help' values are read from chart labels in the order shown and match the report text (56% of Reps say hurt, 52% of Dems say help). No race, gender or age breakdown found for the carbon tax item.

pew_item: Please indicate whether you would favor or oppose the following proposals about gun policy. h. Allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit
notes: Numbers also appear on https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-views-of-specific-gun-policy-proposals/. Topline for the permitless item: 11 strongly favor, 13 somewhat favor, 16 somewhat oppose, 59 strongly oppose. The report charts use Rep/Lean Rep and Dem/Lean Dem. Gun owners 41, non-owners 14. Related item g, 'Allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places', may fit 'expanding concealed carry' better: 44% favor overall (19 strongly + 25 somewhat), Rep 71, owners 68, non-owners 31; Dems are given only as 'fewer than three-in-ten', so no exact Dem number. The report text gives no breakdown by race, gender, age or religion for either item (chart labels are images).

pew_item: As you may know, some colleges and universities around the country are selective, which means they have many more applicants than they can admit. One of the factors some of these colleges take into account in admissions decisions is race and ethnicity, in order to increase the racial and ethnic diversity of the school. All in all, do you approve or disapprove of selective colleges and universities doing this?
notes: Wording and overall 33% are from the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/06/PP_2023.06.08_college-admissions_TOPLINE.pdf); the overall figure also appears on the overview page. Partisan groups include leaners. Ages 50+: 58% disapprove, with approve not reported, so no 50_64 or 65_plus. Approve by education: postgrad 52, bachelor's 40, some college 30, HS or less 26. White Rep 11, Hispanic Rep 28, White Dem 59, Black Dem 50, Hispanic Dem 48, Asian Dem 48. No gender, religion or geography breakdown in the text (chart labels are images). Surveyed before the June 2023 SFFA ruling.

pew_item: In general, do you think that focusing on increasing diversity, equity and inclusion at [work is mainly a good thing, a bad thing, or neither good nor bad]?
notes: The base is workers, not all adults: employed, not self-employed, at organizations with 10+ people (n=4,744), so all_adults holds the all-workers figure. Partisan groups include leaners. The bracketed end of the wording is filled in from Pew's report summary ('mainly a good thing'); the topline text breaks at that point. Responses: 56 good, 16 bad, 28 neither. The item is about DEI efforts in general, not mandatory training or feeling fairly treated. Training-specific item DEITRAIN2, asked only of workers who attended DEI training (n=2,086): 'Overall, would you say the diversity, equity or inclusion trainings you have participated [in have been helpful or unhelpful]', 53% very/somewhat helpful (15+38); Dem 66, Rep 36, women 60, men 46. Education ('good thing'): postgrad 68, bachelor's 59, some college or less 50. Newer reading (Oct 7-13, 2024; https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/11/19/views-of-dei-have-become-slightly-more-negative-among-us-workers/): 52% good overall, men 44, Asian 57; other groups not given exactly, so 2023 is used. Topline: https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/05/ST_2023.05.17_Culture-of-Work-DEI_Topline.pdf

pew_item: Please indicate whether you would favor or oppose each of the following proposals about policing in this country. b. Make it a crime for police to use chokeholds or strangleholds
notes: all_adults = 49 strongly + 25 somewhat favor from the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2020/07/PP_2020.07.09_qualified-immunity_topline.pdf); the report text gives no single overall figure, only 'similar shares' to three-quarters. Group numbers come from the report page; partisan groups include leaners. Strongly favor: Black 74, White 44. No Asian, gender or age breakdown given. The item is a chokehold ban, which is a use-of-force restriction; it does not ask about resident complaints. Other items in the same battery: civilian oversight boards 75% favor (43+32), federal misconduct database 89 (62+27), nonviolent-alternatives training 93 (71+22).

pew_item: Acceptability of family arrangement: 'A married gay or lesbian couple raising children together'
notes: Asks whether a same-sex couple raising children is an acceptable family arrangement, not about adoption policy or foster agencies. The item label is the report's wording; the topline was not read, so the full question stem was not checked. Group numbers are from the report text (report PDF: https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/09/ST_2023.09.14_Modern-Family_Report.pdf). 59 = 47 completely + 12 somewhat acceptable. Ages 50+ are given only as 'about half'. Women are said to be more accepting than men, but no numbers are given. No exact party figure for this item. Related item (unmarried gay/lesbian couple raising children): 53% acceptable overall, Dem/lean Dem 72, Rep/lean Rep 35, LGB 88, straight 50. By marital status: cohabiting 75, married 54, never married 68. Asian figures represent English speakers only. Pew last asked favor/oppose on gay adoption in 2013 or earlier (search results show 52% favor in 2012); that item was not opened, and no 2020+ adoption policy item was found.

pew_item: Here are some current laws and policies that are either in place or being considered in the U.S. related to transgender issues. Would you favor or oppose laws or policies that do each of the following? a. Protect transgender individuals from discrimination in jobs, housing, and public spaces such as restaurants and stores
notes: Covers only protections for transgender people, not LGB people or LGBTQ people broadly; it is a national law/policy question, not a local ordinance, and says nothing about small businesses. Partisan groups include leaners (chart labels Rep/Lean Rep, Dem/Lean Dem). The Rep/Dem figures appear in the report text and match the chart; ages are from the report text. The report says White Democrats are more likely than Black, Hispanic and Asian Democrats to favor protections, but gives no race numbers. Newer reading (Feb 10-17, 2025; topline https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/02/SR_24.02.26_transgender-policies_topline.pdf): 56% favor (31 strongly + 25 favor), down from 64 in 2022 (37+27); the 2025 short read gives no group breakdown, so 2022 is used.

pew_item: Do you think that parents should be able to opt their children out of learning about the following topics in school if the way these topics are taught conflicts with the [parents'] personal views or beliefs? b. Sexual orientation or gender identity
response: No, parents should not be able to opt their children out
notes: Measures support for keeping LGBTQ topics mandatory (no parental opt-out), not support for an inclusive curriculum itself or whether students feel safe. 'should not be able to' is the pro-inclusion direction. The topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2024/02/ST_24.02.22_lgbtq-race-in-schools_topline.pdf) shows 54 yes / 31 no / 13 not sure; one word of the stem was lost in extraction and is bracketed. Party figures are from chart labels (Rep/Lean Rep 11 should-not, 79 should; Dem/Lean Dem 51 should-not, 32 should); the 'should' values match the report text. Among Democrats, should-not: White 60, Asian 53, Hispanic 42, Black 34. The report says overall race differences are small but gives no numbers. Related item (Feb 10-17, 2025, transgender-policies topline): 'Make it illegal for public school districts to teach about gender identity in elementary schools': 47 favor (35+12), 34 oppose (14+20). In 2022: 41 favor, 38 oppose; favor by party Rep 69, Dem 18; by age 18-29 30, 30-49 40, 50+ 46 (2022 report chart).

pew_item: Would you favor or oppose the federal government doing each of the following for people who are providing care for an aging family member? c. Requiring employers to provide paid family leave
notes: Framed around caring for an aging family member, not leave for new parents, and asks about a federal employer mandate rather than return-to-work effects. Topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/02/ST_2026.2.26_family-caregivers_topline.pdf): 44 strongly favor, 25 somewhat, 13 neither, 5 somewhat oppose, 4 strongly oppose, 8 not sure. Party figures (leaners included) are from the report page; no race, gender or age breakdown is given. Pew's closest parental-leave items are from 2017 (https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2017/03/23/americans-widely-support-paid-family-and-medical-leave-but-differ-over-specific-policies/; search snippet: 51% say the federal government should require employers to provide paid leave). That page was not opened, so its numbers are not verified and not recorded.

pew_item: What type of impact do you think having each of the following has had where you work? e. A way for employees to see the salary range for all positions
notes: Not a pay-transparency law question and nothing about the gender pay gap. Asked only of workers whose employer has a salary-range system (n=1,558; 30% of workers report one), so all_adults holds the figure for that worker subgroup. 60 = 31 very + 29 somewhat positive per the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2023/05/ST_2023.05.17_Culture-of-Work-DEI_Topline.pdf); the remainder is 31 neither, 6 somewhat negative, 1 very negative. Party figures (with leaners) are from the report page. No race, gender or age breakdown for this item. Searches found no Pew item on laws requiring employers to disclose pay ranges.

pew_item: Here are some current laws and policies that are either in place or being considered in the U.S. related to transgender issues. Would you favor or oppose laws or policies that do each of the following? d. Require that transgender athletes compete on teams that match the sex they were assigned at birth, not the gender they identify with
notes: DIRECTION: a 'favor' answer supports restricting trans athletes to teams matching their sex at birth. The current (2025-26) federal Title IX athletics position (the Feb 2025 executive order, Education Dept enforcement, NCAA policy) is this restrictive direction, so % favor = support for the 'new Title IX athletics policy'. If the study means the Biden-era proposed rule allowing gender-identity-based participation, the matching share is % oppose: 15 overall (7 oppose + 8 strongly oppose). The topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/02/SR_24.02.26_transgender-policies_topline.pdf) shows 49 strongly favor, 17 favor, 19 neither, 7 oppose, 8 strongly oppose; Form 1 half sample only (the other half saw experimental wording). Party is as reported in the short read (2022: Rep 85, Dem 37; 2022 overall 58; ages 18-29/30-49/50+ in 2022 chart: 43/58/64). Related item with full breakdown (Nov 17-30, 2025, same short read), 'How comfortable would you be with transgender athletes competing on sports teams that do not match their sex at birth?', not too/not at all comfortable: total 73, Rep 91, Dem 55, men 77, women 69, White 75, Black 68, Hispanic 67, Asian 68, 18-29 60, 30-49 70, 50-64 79, 65+ 80, LGBTQ 34.

pew_item: Favor/oppose public schools allowing: students voluntarily praying in student-led groups (item label as shown in Pew short read; verbatim questionnaire PDF could not be parsed)
notes: Item is student-led voluntary prayer in student-led groups (not specifically 'at school events'). Partisan groups include leaners. Catholic is all Catholics. Regions also reported: South 82, Midwest 80, Northeast 75, West 73 (no urban/suburban/rural). Same survey: teachers leading classes in prayer favor 46% overall; coaches leading teams in prayer favor 57% (Rep 77, Dem 38, white evangelical 89, Catholic 64, unaffiliated 28). Wording taken from short-read chart labels; questionnaire at https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/06/SR_26.06.22_school-prayer_questionnaire.pdf not readable.

pew_item: And if you had to choose, which comes closest to your view? Businesses that provide wedding services, such as catering or flowers should be: able to refuse to provide those services to same-sex couples if the business owner has religious objections to homosexuality, OR required to provide those services to same-sex couples just as they would to all other customers?
response: Able to refuse (i.e., favor the religious exemption)
notes: OLDER ITEM (2016); no 2020+ Pew item found. Item is a religious exemption from serving same-sex weddings for businesses (not specifically faith-based service providers such as adoption/social-service agencies). 49% chose 'required'. Catholic = all Catholics. Gender reported only for 'required' (women 54, men 44), not for 'able to refuse', so omitted. Overview page: https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2016/09/28/where-the-public-stands-on-religious-liberty-vs-nondiscrimination/ ; numbers read from report PDF chart table.

No Pew public-opinion item on school vouchers / public funding for private or religious schools found. Pew's 2019 religion-in-schools report explicitly excludes vouchers; 2002/2003/2009 Pew pages are legal analyses. A 2009 Pew 'School Vouchers' PDF package (https://assets.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2009/12/VoucherPackage.pdf) could not be read and appears to compile others' polling.

pew_item: Whether the federal government has a responsibility to ensure all Americans have a high-speed internet connection at home during the COVID-19 outbreak (paraphrase; verbatim wording not printed on page)
response: Yes, it is the federal government's responsibility
notes: Approximate: government responsibility to ensure home high-speed internet (pandemic framing), not a rural broadband subsidy. Overall yes not given exactly ('about four-in-ten'; 62% say not the government's responsibility), so all_adults left null. Urban/suburban/rural figures for this April 2020 survey read on https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/08/19/some-digital-divides-persist-between-rural-urban-and-suburban-america/ . April 2021 repeat: 37% yes, Dem 54, Rep 18 (https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2021/09/01/navigating-technological-challenges/). Separate April 5-11, 2021 item without pandemic framing: 43% say federal government has a responsibility to provide access to high-speed internet for all Americans (no subgroups on page; https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/05/17/americans-see-broad-responsibilities-for-government-little-change-since-2019/). Partisan groups include leaners.

pew_item: Whether it is the right thing or wrong thing for the government to reduce agricultural subsidies to most farms (paraphrase of Obama budget proposal item; verbatim wording not printed)
field_dates: Report published March 16, 2009 (field dates not shown on page)
notes: OLDER ITEM (2009); no 2020+ Pew item on farm subsidies/payments found (incl. 2025 tariff-related farm aid). Direction is reversed: % supports cutting subsidies, not supporting them. Republicans: 34% right thing, 57% wrong thing; key used is rep_lean_rep but page says 'Republicans' (likely excludes leaners). Democrats and independents described only as 'more evenly divided', no numbers.

pew_item: As I read some possible government policies to address America's energy supply, tell me whether you would favor or oppose each. ... Would you favor or oppose the government [spending more on subway, rail and bus systems]?
notes: OLDER ITEM (2012); no 2020+ Pew transit-funding item found. Asked in an energy-policy battery. Partisan groups here are Republicans/Democrats WITHOUT leaners, with independents shown separately (keys reused). 31% oppose. Report page: https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2012/03/19/as-gas-prices-pinch-support-for-oil-and-gas-production-grows/ . Related recent but broader item: Sept. 2021, 51% favored the $1.2T Senate-passed infrastructure bill (not transit-specific).

pew_item: Gradually raising the age at which people can begin to receive Social Security benefits (paraphrase on page; verbatim wording not printed)
notes: OLDER ITEM (2012); no 2020+ Pew item on raising the retirement age found (2024 Pew survey: 79% say benefits shouldn't be reduced in any way, per https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/05/20/what-the-data-says-about-social-security/ -- a different item). 56% oppose. Asked of half sample. Party numbers not given (Republicans and independents more supportive than Democrats, none majority).
No Pew public-opinion item on federal student loan forgiveness/cancellation found; Pew's student-loan topic pages and 2024 fact pieces are descriptive (debt levels), not opinion on forgiveness.

No Pew item on allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices found (searches returned only KFF/Gallup/YouGov/AARP, which are excluded). Closest Pew items are 2004-2006 views of the Medicare Part D law, not negotiation.

pew_item: [Do you approve] or disapprove of each of the following? ... Using state and local law enforcement to help with federal efforts to deport people who are in the U.S. illegally (topline item LOCSTATE; opening words of stem not cleanly extracted from topline PDF)
notes: Overall 50% approve / 49% disapprove (topline: 25 strongly approve, 25 somewhat approve, 20 somewhat disapprove, 29 strongly disapprove; topline https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/06/PP_2025-6-17_trump-immigration_topline.pdf; overall figure also on https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/17/americans-have-mixed-to-negative-views-of-trump-administration-immigration-actions/). Asked of Form 2 (N=2,530). Item is local law enforcement helping federal deportation (close match to local-ICE partnerships). Dem/lean Dem, Black, Hispanic and under-50 exact figures not stated in text (only 'no more than a quarter', 'about a third', 'fewer than four-in-ten', 'about four-in-ten'), so omitted. Partisan groups include leaners. No gender/religion breakdowns.

pew_item: Favor/oppose laws and policies that would: Require health insurance companies to cover medical care for gender transitions (item label as shown in short read; verbatim wording not printed on page)
notes: Item is not age-specific (covers anyone, incl. adults) and is about insurance coverage of transition care, not access to care per se, hence approximate. 53% oppose/strongly oppose; down 5 pts from 27% favor in May 2022. No subgroups shown for this item. Same survey, minors-specific item: 'Ban health care professionals from providing care related to gender transitions for minors' favor 56% (Rep/lean Rep 79, Dem/lean Dem 35) -- a minors item, opposite direction.

pew_item: As you may know, the Affordable Care Act requires that many employer-provided health insurance plans cover the cost of a wide variety of birth control options. Some argue that employers who have a religious objection to the use of birth control should be able to refuse to provide it in health insurance plans for their employees. Others argue that [they] should be required to provide it in health insurance plans for their employees, just as other employers are required to do. ... if you had to choose, which comes closest to your view?
notes: OLDER ITEM (2016) and approximate: about the ACA employer birth-control coverage mandate even for employers with religious objections, not a government-funded free-contraception program. 30% chose 'able to refuse'. Final forced-choice wording reconstructed from topline intro + chart label ('Employers who have a religious objection to the use of birth control should be ____ to provide it in health insurance plans for employees'). Catholic = all Catholics. No 2020+ Pew item on contraception coverage/funding found.

No pewresearch.org survey item on charter schools or school choice from 2020 or later found. The only one found is the 2004 Pew Hispanic Center/Kaiser National Survey of Latinos: Education (fielded 8/7/03-10/15/03; https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/reports/25.pdf). That PDF is encrypted and could not be read, and the HTML pages do not show the charter item, so no numbers are recorded. Search snippets gave figures, but they were not used under rule 2.

Several pewresearch.org searches (cash bail, bail reform, pretrial detention) found no survey item on bail. Related Pew items, such as whether people spend too much or too little time in prison (2021) and whether the justice system is tough enough (2024), are different policies and were not used.

No pewresearch.org item on zoning or allowing apartments in single-family neighborhoods found. Pew Research Center asks about preferred community type (big houses farther apart vs. smaller walkable), which is a different construct. A zoning-reform survey (Sept 2023, Ipsos KnowledgePanel) exists, but it is from The Pew Charitable Trusts (pew.org), a separate organization. It was excluded under rule 1 (pewresearch.org only) and not opened.

pew_item: Is it the federal government's responsibility to make sure all Americans have health care coverage?
notes: Approximate: this asks about a general federal responsibility to ensure coverage for all Americans, not Medicaid expansion for low-income adults. No pewresearch.org item on Medicaid expansion found. The only recent Pew Medicaid item found is on work requirements (2025: 49% favor), which is a different policy and has no group breakdown on the page read. Partisan groups include leaners. Asian figures are English speakers only. The page also reports education and income groups. Gender, religion and community type are not reported. Sample: 10,357 ATP adults.

pew_item: Which of the following would you prefer that this child learn in school, even if neither is exactly right? [That not having sex (abstinence) is the only safe and effective way to prevent unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) / That there are methods of contraception that are safe and effective ways to prevent unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) / Child should not learn about this in school]
response: That there are methods of contraception that are safe and effective ways to prevent unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
notes: Sample is parents of K-12 children who are not homeschooled (n=3,039 for this item), not all adults. Total among these parents is 59%, which is why all_adults is null. men/women are fathers and mothers, from the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2022/10/ST_2022.10.26_Parents-K-12_TOPLINE.pdf). Contraception content is a proxy for comprehensive sex ed vs. abstinence-only, not a direct policy question. Partisan groups include leaners. Race breakdowns exist only among Democratic parents (White 84, Black 51, Hispanic 63), so they are not recorded as race groups. Read from the report text and the report/topline PDFs fetched from pewresearch.org.

pew_item: Do you favor or oppose allowing churches and other houses of worship, along with other organizations, to apply for government funding to provide social services such as job training or drug treatment counseling? (wording as paraphrased in the report text; full questionnaire not read)
notes: OLD ITEM (2009); no newer pewresearch.org item found. The item covers government funding of faith-based social services in general (job training, drug treatment), not prisoner reentry specifically. The page gives no exact question text, only a close paraphrase. The page says 'Republicans' and 'Democrats'; it does not state whether leaners are included, and in 2009 phone surveys they were probably not. 'catholic' is white non-Hispanic Catholics. 18_29 is 'under 30'. Other age bands, independents, gender and unaffiliated are not reported. 25% oppose overall. Phone survey, N=4,013.

pew_item: Which comes closer to your view about the use of marijuana by adults?
response: It should be legal for medical AND recreational use
notes: Question wording is from the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/05/SR_26.05.26_marijuana_topline.pdf). Options: legal for medical AND recreational / medical ONLY (33%) / NOT legal (11%). The item measures support for the policy; it says nothing about the opioid claim. Asian figures are English speakers only. The page also reports 65-74 (50), 75+ (34) and ideology-within-party groups. Gender, religion and community type are not reported. N=8,512.

pew_item: Would you favor or oppose the federal government doing each of the following to encourage more people to have children? a. Providing free child care
notes: Approximate in three ways. (1) It was asked only of the 32% of adults who said the federal government should have a major or minor role in encouraging births (n=2,726), so all_adults is null. Within that subset the topline (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/09/SR_25.09.30_Pronatalism_topline.pdf) shows 36% strongly and 28% somewhat favor, and the report says 'more than six-in-ten'. (2) It is free child care, not a subsidy. (3) It is framed as a pronatalist policy, not help for parents returning to work. The partisan figures are within the same subset; the report says Republicans/Democrats, and its other figures include leaners. No pewresearch.org item on child care subsidies for all adults found.

No pewresearch.org item on government funding for rural hospitals or rural health care found. Pew has a 2018 analysis of distance to the nearest hospital and an item on access to good doctors and hospitals as a local problem; neither is a policy-support item.

pew_item: Preventing people with mental illnesses from purchasing guns (gun policy proposal; favor/oppose)
notes: Approximate: this is a purchase ban for people with mental illness, not a red flag law or ERPO (a court order to temporarily remove guns someone already owns because they are judged a risk). No pewresearch.org item on red flag laws or ERPOs found. Consider treating this as not_found if a close match is required. The exact question stem was not shown on the page. Field dates are from the main report page (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/gun-violence-widely-viewed-as-a-major-and-growing-national-problem/), which says its partisan groups include leaners. Gun owners 87%, non-owners 89%. N=5,115.

No pewresearch.org item on bilingual or dual-language instruction for English learners found. A March 2026 Pew item asks how important it is for U.S. children to learn a language other than English (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/03/what-do-americans-think-about-language-learning-in-us-schools/). That is foreign-language learning, a different policy, so it was not used.
